notes:
I've gathered enough for most verses but couldn't cover all of them. **Gaps:** I found nothing about the tune "The Lilies," and little on vv. 5, 8, 12 and 15. I didn't reach the NET Bible notes or any Lutheran site. The only Lutheran view I have is secondhand, and I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm, so those are left out. **Numbering:** the Hebrew text and Catholic/Orthodox Bibles number this psalm one verse higher than the BSB (and Catholic/Orthodox Bibles call it Psalm 44). I've converted everything to BSB numbering.

## Overview (whole psalm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The psalm is a royal wedding song about an earthly king that ultimately celebrates Christ. The bride is the Church, called to leave everything and be united with Him.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
  - It can't be tied firmly to one Davidic king. Many older commentators regard the wedding as Solomon's to the Princess of Egypt, but this is not certain. (same URL)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** He sees no earthly wedding at all: "This is no wedding song of earthly nuptials, but an Epithalamium for the Heavenly Bridegroom and his elect spouse." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps045.cfm
- **Maclaren (also Baptist):** He holds to a real historical wedding. The psalm has a prelude (v. 1), an address to the groom (vv. 2–9), an address to the bride (vv. 10–15) and a closing prediction.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-two/psalm-forty-five.cfm
- **Bible.org (Utley), a modern evangelical view:** Candidates for the king include Solomon, Ahab (married to Jezebel, a princess of Tyre), David, and the Messiah (Ibn Ezra's second choice and the Church Fathers' view). It treats the psalm as Messianic "only in a typological sense" and notes it fits the exaggerated royal language of the ancient Near East. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45
- **Seedbed (Wesleyan):** At its simplest it is a song for a king's marriage. But on a deeper level, it reminds us that marriage has always been a sacrament—i.e., an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace. https://seedbed.com/the-marriage-of-heaven-and-earth-psalm-45/
- **Augustine (Catholic, via New Advent):** The psalm is about the sacred marriage feast: Christ the Bridegroom and the Church the Bride. The "bridechamber" of the union of the Word and flesh was the Virgin's womb. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801045.htm

## v. 1
- **Enduring Word:** The poem is either *about* the king or *to* him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
  - Guzik cites Maclaren: the Hebrew says "a king," without "the," "suggesting that the office is more prominent than the person." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-45.cfm
- **Bible.org:** This is the only place in the Psalms where the author describes himself. "Ready writer" may mean he was eager to praise, or that he was a court poet or scribe. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45
- **Augustine (Catholic):** Some take "my heart has uttered a good word" as spoken by the Father, pointing to the eternal begetting of the Son, the Word. Others read it simply as the prophet writing a hymn. "Writing quickly" may mean writing of things soon to come, since God did not wait long to reveal Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801045.htm

## v. 2
- **Enduring Word:** The king's beauty is of character, not looks, since Isaiah 53:2 says the Messiah was not physically striking. His gracious lips speak words full of grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
  - Guzik quotes Horne: Christ's word "instructed the ignorant, resolved the doubtful, comforted the mourners, reclaimed the wicked" https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-45.cfm
- **Bible.org:** The word for "fairer" is rarely used of men. It cautions against reading "therefore God has blessed you" as cause and effect: the king held his office by family line, not because he deserved it. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45
- **Augustine:** "Than the children of men" (not "than the angels") shows He was truly a man, though no ordinary one. He links "grace on your lips" with John 1:17. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801045.htm

## vv. 3–5
- **Enduring Word:** The gracious king is no weakling but a man of war. His majesty comes from truth, humility and righteousness rather than mere force. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
  - Spurgeon (quoted there): Jesus is "mighty to save, mighty in love."
- **Bible.org:** This is military imagery of a king fighting as God's representative. "Splendor" and "majesty" are often words for God but are also used of Israel's king (Ps 21:5). In vv. 4–5 it is hard to tell which pronouns refer to God and which to the king. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45
- **Augustine:** The sword on the thigh is Christ's word, the sword that divides (Matthew 10:34). Riding on and reigning is fulfilled as nations submit to Him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801045.htm

## v. 6 — the main point of disagreement
- **Traditional "the King is God" reading:**
  - Barnes says Hebrews 1:8 clearly treats this as about the Messiah and "clearly proves that Christ is Divine."
  - Gill insists the verse can't be rendered "thy throne is God" or "thy throne is the throne of God."
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the "O God" reading is backed by the Greek Old Testament (LXX), Hebrews and the Aramaic paraphrase. It calls the anti-Messianic alternatives "wholly untenable."
  - URLs: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/45-6.htm and https://biblehub.com/psalms/45-6.htm
- **Enduring Word:** Here God praises the Messiah as God. Hebrews shows these are words of God the Father to God the Son. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-45.cfm
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** The Christian use in Hebrews doesn't explain how the earthly king could be called God. He offers "Thy throne is of God for ever" as grammatically preferable. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/psalms/45-6.html
- **The Expositor's Bible:** The psalm does point to Christ, "But we cannot take the ascription of the title "O God" as having reference to His Divine nature." (same URL)
- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Christ ensures that David's throne is the throne of God, because Jesus, the son of David, is the incarnate Lord. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/kings-glorious-bride
- **Bible.org (modern view):** The variety of translations shows the Hebrew is uncertain ("your divine throne," "God has enthroned you," and others). In the Old Testament's belief in one God it can't call the king divine; Hebrews uses it as royal typology. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45
- **Ellicott on Hebrews 1:8:** The ancient Jewish Targum took the psalm as addressed to the King Messiah. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/1-8.htm

## v. 7
- **Enduring Word:** The verse shows the Trinity at work. "God, your God" is the Father, "you" is the Son, and "anointed" points to the Holy Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
- **Bible.org:** Verse 7 itself shows that v. 6 isn't calling an Israelite king divine. Whether the praise was true depends on the king: hyperbole if Ahab, true at first if Solomon. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45

## v. 8
- **Maclaren:** The psalm now reaches the wedding itself. The king's robes are so perfumed they seem woven of fragrance, and music greets him as he approaches the ivory palaces. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-two/psalm-forty-five.cfm
- **Bible.org:** "Cassia" appears only here in the Old Testament and may be a cinnamon-like spice. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45

## v. 9
- **Gill:** The queen is the Church, the Lamb's wife. Her title comes from being married to Christ, not from herself. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/psalms/45-9.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The right hand was the place of honor; Solomon gave it to the queen mother, Bathsheba (1 Kings 2:19). https://biblehub.com/psalms/45-9.htm
- **Maclaren:** He warns against finding Christ in every detail. The lesser royal wives can only refer to the actual historical occasion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-two/psalm-forty-five.cfm
- **Bishop Horsley (Anglican), a distinctive view:** The queen is the Hebrew Church, Israel restored to Christ by conversion. The kings' daughters are the Gentile churches gathered in the meantime. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/45-9.htm
- **Augustine:** The kings' daughters are cities that received the faith, such as Rome and Carthage, and "all these make up one single Queen." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801045.htm

## vv. 10–11
- **Enduring Word:** This echoes Genesis 2:24. Since Jesus never married, it fits the picture of God's people as His bride. "Worship Him" means more than the respect owed a husband. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
- **Maclaren:** The bride must revere the king as well as love him. He admits this reflects an old-fashioned view of marriage but applies it to souls approaching Jesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-two/psalm-forty-five.cfm
- **Bible.org:** These verses show the bride was foreign, which could fit David, Solomon or Ahab. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45
- **Augustine:** Prophets and apostles, as "fathers," speak these words to the Church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801045.htm
- **Orthodox use:** The words "Hearken, O daughter" are used as a verse in the shared services for feasts of the Virgin Mary (Theotokos). https://www.ccel.org/ccel/anonymous/menaion.v.html
  - The same words appear in an OCA prokeimenon (a sung verse before a Scripture reading). https://www.oca.org/files/PDF/Music/Akathists/Sitka/Sitka-prokeimenonandleteverybreath.pdf

## v. 12
- **Enduring Word:** Being joined to the king brings the bride gifts from the nations. Kidner (quoted there): "she is gainer, not the loser, by her homage." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
- **Bible.org:** The mention of Tyre fits Ahab's marriage to Jezebel, a Tyrian princess. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45

## v. 13
- **Enduring Word:** She is "all glorious" because of her union with the King, not because of herself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-45/
- **Spurgeon:** The Church is royal by birth and renewed in nature. Her clothing of gold is Christ's righteousness worked into a garment for His people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/45-13.htm
  - He also says "within" may mean her real charms lie in her heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps045.cfm
- **Barnes:** At the literal level she is the foreign king's daughter, still in her father's palace before being taken to her husband. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/45-13.html
- **Bible.org:** The Hebrew reads "within," but some scholars suggest "pearls"; the UBS Text Project rates the Hebrew reading "A." https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45
- **Augustine:** Her robe is gold outwardly, but the One who loved her also knew she was beautiful within. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801045.htm

## vv. 14–15
- **Spurgeon:** This is the final wedding procession, when the Lamb's bride will be seen by the whole universe. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps045.cfm
- **Maclaren:** The virgin companions don't spoil the Christ-and-Church reading any more than the ten virgins spoil Jesus' parable. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-two/psalm-forty-five.cfm
- **Bible.org:** These verses describe the bridal party, and the Church later applied this section to herself, as she did with the Song of Songs. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45

## v. 16
- **Enduring Word:** The words now address the king (Kidner notes "you" is masculine). The marriage produces sons who become princes, as in Hebrews 2:10's "many sons brought to glory." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-45.cfm
- **Spurgeon:** Christ had royal ancestors back to Jesse, and now the Eternal King has "sons" (believers) who will reign. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps045.cfm
- **Bible.org (quoting the UBS Handbook):** The literal sense is a promise of many sons who will be kings. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-45

## v. 17
- **Matthew Henry:** The Father keeps Christ's name alive through a succession of ministers and Christians in every age. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/45-13.html
- **Boice (quoted by Guzik):** He asks whether we, like the psalmist, are praising Christ and working for the nations to honor Him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-45.cfm

## Where the traditions differ
1. **Literal wedding or pure prophecy?**
   - Spurgeon reads it as purely about Christ.
   - Maclaren keeps a real wedding plus a reference to Christ.
   - Guzik/Kidner hold both levels at once.
   - Utley sees typology only.
   - The split runs within traditions: Spurgeon and Maclaren are both Baptists.
2. **"O God" in v. 6:** direct proof of Christ's deity (Barnes, Gill, Pulpit) versus an Anglican (Ellicott) and Expositor's Bible caution, and the modern view (Utley).
3. **Who is the queen/bride?**
   - The Church: Gill, Spurgeon, Augustine.
   - Restored Israel: Horsley.
   - Luther (reported secondhand in that Horsley sermon) took her as the whole Church of Jews and Gentiles.
   - Orthodox worship applies v. 10 to Mary.
4. **Marriage as "sacrament":** Seedbed (Wesleyan) uses the psalm this way, which the Baptist and Reformed sources I read don't do.
